newsitem.title: USA: April leading index posts first fall in a year.
newsitem.headline: April leading index posts first fall in a year.

text.p: A key gauge of economic activity fell for the first time in 15 months in April, the Conference Board said Tuesday, a sign of potentially slower growth in coming months.

The Index of Leading Indicators, meant to forecast economic trends six to nine months ahead, fell 0.1 percent in April -- the first decline since a 0.7 percent decline in January 1996 -- after a revised 0.2 percent rise in March, the business research group said.
It said six of the index's 10 components contributed to the weaker reading in April. Among them were a rise in new jobless claims, lower stock prices and a drop in consumer confidence.

The report added to recent signs the economy may be slowing after its rapid growth in the first quarter. Recent reports have showed weaker retail sales in April and flat industrial output, as well as sluggish car sales.
However, the nation's purchasing managers said Monday that a widely watched index of industrial activity unexpectedly jumped in May even as consumer spending showed signs of easing.

The conflicting signals have left analysts uncertain about whether the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again next month in a bid to slow growth and ward off inflation. The economy grew at a sizzling 5.8 percent rate in the first quarter, though that is expected to slow later in the year.
Fed policy-makers held short-term rates steady last month after raising them a quarter point in March, the first increase in more than two years.

In its report, the board said vendors delivered goods more quickly, a sign that factories were not as busy, and orders for capital goods fell. There also were fewer new applications for building permits.
Only four indicators strengthened in April.
The average workweek lengthened, consumer goods orders rose, the money supply increased and the Treasury yield curve was more favourable.
Previously, the board said the leading index had risen 0.1 percent in March, but it revised that upward.
